title: Who Is Aman Sanger? The 25-Year-Old Son of Indian Immigrants Behind Cursor's $60 Billion SpaceX Deal

body:
Key Takeaways
  • Aman Sanger co-founded Cursor, acquired by SpaceX for $60 billion, at just 25 years old.
  • Cursor reached $1 billion in annual revenue within two years, a record for SaaS companies.
  • Sanger's upbringing combined Indian immigrant values with American entrepreneurial spirit.
  • The acquisition values each co-founder's stake at approximately $2.7 billion.
  • Sanger's journey reflects the potential of the Indian diaspora in tech innovation.
Aman Sanger's Background
›Born to Indian immigrant parents in New York.
›Father: IIT graduate, hedge fund founder.
›Mother: Orthodontist turned entrepreneur.
›Started coding at age 14.
›Excelled in academics and sports at Horace Mann.

In June 2026, SpaceX agreed to acquire Cursor — the AI-powered code editor that has quietly become indispensable to millions of developers — in an all-stock deal valued at $60 billion. It was the largest AI acquisition of the year. At the centre of it stood Aman Sanger, a 25-year-old Indian-American who co-founded the company just four years earlier in an MIT dorm room.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=XBQEdtXjlho

Sanger's reaction on X was characteristically understated: "Excited to train some very strong models!" For someone whose net worth had just crossed an estimated $5.5 billion, it was the kind of response that tells you everything about how he operates — head down, shipping code, letting the product do the talking.

Roots in Two Worlds

Sanger was born in New York to Indian immigrant parents who brought with them a deep emphasis on education and enterprise. His father, Arvind Sanger, graduated from IIT Bombay before earning an MBA at Tulane University and building a career in finance. In 2007, he founded Geosphere Capital, a hedge fund focused on natural resources, industrial sectors, and Indian equities.

His mother, Shilpa Sanger, was raised in Mumbai and trained as an orthodontist before becoming an entrepreneur and angel investor. She also serves on the board of Pratham USA, the education nonprofit that works to improve learning outcomes for children across India.

It was this household — where IIT rigour met American entrepreneurship — that shaped what came next. Sanger started coding at 14. At Horace Mann School, he captained the squash team, earned two-time All-American honours, and won both the Athlete of the Year and American Chemical Society awards. He was, by every measure, the kind of kid who could have coasted into any conventional career. He chose to build instead.

![Horace Mann. › Excelled in academics and sports at Horace Mann.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4e/Southworth_and_Hawes_-_Horace_Mann_%28Zeno_Fotografie%29_%28cropped%29.jpg)

MIT and the Seeds of Cursor

Sanger enrolled at MIT in 2018 to study computer science and mathematics. The four years that followed were formative in ways that went far beyond coursework. He interned at Google and Bridgewater Associates, ran a small AI consultancy on the side, and co-authored a paper published in Nature Methods on Tangram, a deep-learning framework for computational biology.

"A lot of the work for Cursor has been just experimenting with what is possible. For everything that you may see in the product, there's ten failed experiments of what didn't work."

— Aman Sanger

More importantly, he met Michael Truell, Sualeh Asif, and Arvid Lunnemark — the three classmates who would become his co-founders. Asif, a Karachi-born mathematics prodigy and three-time International Mathematical Olympiad medallist, brought deep product intuition. Truell, who would become CEO, brought vision. Lunnemark brought engineering depth. Sanger, who took on the role of Chief Operating Officer, brought the operational instinct that turned their ideas into a company.

Building Cursor

In 2022, the four left MIT and incorporated Anysphere with a modest $400,000 pre-seed cheque. The company initially explored building an AI copilot for the mechanical engineering industry before pivoting to what would become Cursor — an AI-assisted code editor capable of analysing entire codebases and generating complex solutions.

Sanger's LinkedIn bio distils his mission into a single line: "Removing all bottlenecks in creating software."

What made Cursor different was not just the technology but the growth strategy. There was no marketing budget, no sales team, no ad spend. Sanger architected a pure word-of-mouth playbook — build something so good that developers would tell other developers. It worked. By mid-2025, the platform was generating more than one billion accepted lines of code every day. By November 2025, it had crossed $1 billion in annualised revenue. By early June 2026, that figure stood at roughly $4 billion.

Today, developers at some 50,000 enterprises — including Nvidia, Adobe, Uber, Shopify, and PayPal — use Cursor daily. Most SaaS companies take a decade to reach $1 billion in recurring revenue. Cursor did it in about two years.

The SpaceX Chapter

The $60 billion acquisition by SpaceX, announced just four days after the rocket company's record-breaking Nasdaq IPO, valued each co-founder's 4.5 per cent stake at approximately $2.7 billion. Forbes estimates Sanger's total net worth at $5.5 billion, making him one of the youngest self-made billionaires in the world. SpaceX expects to close the merger by the third quarter of 2026.

The SpaceX Acquisition
›Acquisition valued at $60 billion.
›Each co-founder's stake worth approximately $2.7 billion.
›Sanger's net worth estimated at $5.5 billion.
›Merger expected to close by Q3 2026.

Why It Matters

Aman Sanger's story is a distinctly diaspora story. He is the product of an IIT graduate's ambition, a Mumbai-raised mother's enterprise, an American education system's opportunity, and his own relentless execution. He didn't build Cursor to represent anyone — he built it because he saw a problem worth solving. But for the millions of Indian-origin families watching from New Jersey living rooms and Bengaluru apartments alike, the message is hard to miss: one of the defining products of the AI era was built, in part, by one of theirs.
